physicalNotes: Radius 0.7538 (+0.0026/-0.0023) Jupiter radii and mass 0.333 (+0.016/-0.016) Jupiter masses from Doyle et al. (2011, Science 333, 1602; arXiv:1109.3432), Table 1: 53,890.67 km at 71,492 km per Jupiter radius; GM is the mass times Jupiter's GM 126686531.9 km^3/s^2. A sphere: no oblateness is measured.

sources.period: The mean transit period 225.885 d of the Villanova Kepler Eclipsing Binary Catalogue (Kirk et al. 2016, AJ 151, 68) entry for KIC 12644769, read 2026-09-23 from https://keplerebs.villanova.edu/overview/?k=12644769 (its second ephemeris), a linear fit to the Kepler transits of the planet across star A, 2009-2013. Both published periods fail as a fixed-ellipse period: Doyle et al.'s 228.776 d is osculating at 2010 and 'will vary by approximately +/-5 days over a timescale of just years' (Triaud et al. (2022, MNRAS 511, 3561; arXiv:2112.06584), Table 2, the adopted Kima column, Sect. 3.5), and misplaces the Kepler transits by up to 19 d; Triaud et al.'s mean 226.0 +/- 1.7 d carries a phase uncertain by 92 d. With Doyle et al.'s phase, this period puts all seven Kepler transits across A within 0.13 d of their observed times.
sources.shape: Doyle et al. (2011, Science 333, 1602; arXiv:1109.3432), Table 1: a2 = 0.7048 (+0.0011/-0.0011) au over A's 451,439.73 km radius: 233.55627 stellar radii; i2 = 90.0322 (+0.0022/-0.0023) degrees. This osculating axis is 0.9% larger than Kepler's third law gives for the mean period; the binary's pull on the planet makes that difference, and a fixed ellipse cannot hold both.
sources.phase: Derived from Doyle et al. (2011, Science 333, 1602; arXiv:1109.3432), Table 1: the mean anomaly M2 = lambda2 - omega2 - Omega2 = 106.51 - 318 - 0.003 = 148.507 degrees at BJD 2,455,212.12316 (BJD_TDB), so periastron falls M2/360 of the mean period (93.183 d) earlier: BMJD_TDB 55118.44121. The osculating mean longitude places the planet at that date to 0.3 degrees; the mean period carries it on. Checked against the seven Kepler transits across A in packages/astronomy/src/hostedOrbits.test.ts, which it matches within 0.13 d while single transits alternate by about 2.3 d either way as A swings around the barycentre.
sources.orientation: Doyle et al. (2011, Science 333, 1602; arXiv:1109.3432), Table 1: Omega2 = 0.003 +/- 0.013 degrees, measured from the binary's node, which this package puts at position angle 0 by display convention (see kepler-16-b); the planet's node is entered 0.003 degrees further.
sources.argumentOfPeriapsis: Doyle et al. (2011, Science 333, 1602; arXiv:1109.3432), Table 1: omega2 = 318 (+10/-22) degrees, in the convention of omega1 (star A's side). With e2 = 0.0069 it moves the planet by under half a degree.
sources.barycentre: The Jacobian orbit is about the centre of mass of A and B, weighted by the masses of Doyle et al. (2011, Science 333, 1602; arXiv:1109.3432), Table 1: 0.20255 / (0.6897 + 0.20255) = 0.22701 of the way from A to B.
